title: 100K Users, a $10B Valuation: Personal Agents Are Priced Ahead of Their Products
dek: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and hasn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50M to $10B in six months — in this round of personal-agent hype, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
why: Four frontline product people break down four routes — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse — and also explain why that earlier batch of products, the crayfish ones, became martyrs. High information density, but the second half is worth more.
who: Product managers, investors and engineers watching AI application-layer startups, especially anyone building or about to build a personal assistant and needing to judge this round's valuations and product cadence.
skip: The 01:31 to 01:45 segment with the North American junior-year founder is mostly fundraising narrative, with information density clearly below the segments around it.

points.body: Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation went from $50M at the start of the year to $500M in August, then $2.5B at the end of August, and this month the new round being floated in the market has already reached $10B, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old nobody, with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it will pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

points.h: The line between tool and person is initiative
points.body: The biggest difference between this wave of agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are, like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — setting up an automated task in Manus still depends on prompts, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't initiative. Real initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and comes over on their own to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

points.h: Office agents organize by project, personal agents by person
points.body: The core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along the dimension of a mission or project, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centered on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks — it's office agents that really care about task completion rates.

points.h: Town starts by trading email for the user's mandate
points.body: All four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile client, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-files them, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends them automatically once you confirm. It goes deeper on the email scenario than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and acquire the user's ultimate mandate bit by bit.

points.h: Poke didn't break out for reasons other than technology
points.body: Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could have done it at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-mandate route, able to access credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you — things users had never seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it never took the step of "getting things done for you."

points.h: Cloud agents must handle three environments
points.body: Mark says building a cloud agent was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely different things. To build personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable the moment the computer screen goes off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between those three environments are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably in the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

points.h: Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two businesses
points.body: Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like paying for a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and short on time and energy. Muse is more like a middleman, a shopping guide, an agent — although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, aimed at mass users, blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, and the scenarios they cut into and the users they filter out are different too.

points.h: For an agent, your saved folder may be noise
points.body: The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was: extract what you like to eat from the ingredients saved on Instagram, generate a shopping list, adjust the menu by dinner party size and dietary restrictions, then complete the shopping and the relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is face-saving for the free business narrative: helping users complete transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want solved; users would rather solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in saved folders — the truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

points.h: GUI is a maze map for ordinary people
points.body: Today didn't originally want to make a standalone app; it was very channel-heavy, plugged into WeChat and Telegram, with most scenarios completed inside the channel. But it soon discovered the discoverability problem: users staring at a blank chat box had no idea what to do. So it had to step into GUI, and doing GUI requires a standalone app, and in the end it still built chat into the app. Suki's takeaway is that GUI today no longer carries the user's operation entry point the way it used to; it's more like a map — to ordinary people an agent is more like a maze full of treasure, and GUI gives ordinary people a map of the maze, and following it you can find the treasure.

points.h: If 90% of effort goes to generic capability, pivot
points.body: Suki originally built the AI education product Monspeak, and when doing 2.0 this Spring Festival found that to build a truly personalized teacher, 90% of the effort ended up going into how to make the agent run stably and have personalized memory. If 90% of the effort is going into a very generic capability, then conversely those generic agents might eat the vertical scenario just by finishing it casually. So the judgment was that the consumer track won't end up with that many players — it will be highly concentrated, winner-take-all — and Suki switched to joining a startup to build personal AI together.

points.h: This wave has no network effect to lock users in
points.body: Suki thinks this AI shift is very different from the last mobile internet wave: the biggest change this time is technological innovation, not the narrative of scaling up, burning money and building network effects. There is no network effect or scale effect that can lock users in — as long as your product is good, I'll switch to another one the very next day, because no two-sided network platform has formed, and there's no reason users must stay with you. People stay on Xiaohongshu and Douyin because a two-sided network platform has formed and they can't easily migrate away. So innovative companies are actually easier to fight than in the last mobile internet wave — just hurry to innovate and win users with the best experience.

points.h: The most valuable thing is the processing layer in the middle
points.body: At the end they asked where the most valuable position is in the personal agent era. Suki picks trust and habit — context is only the entry-level foundation; ultimately it's the dependence, habit and trust formed through long-term use; if forced to choose, Suki leans toward the end closer to the user, because model makers are still chasing each other, and the merchant and MCP end will grow naturally with the market. Mark thinks it's neither context nor the ecosystem layer: just getting a lot of context is not nearly enough, it doesn't directly deliver value, and memory is far more complex than imagined — something said last week may already be invalid this week, and if it's still in memory it's serious noise. The most valuable thing is the processing layer in the middle, a bit like Douyin's recommendation algorithm; how the execution mechanism works is each company's secret.

terms.def: An AI that organizes context around the user themselves, understands them over the long term, and proactively gets things done for them.
The engineering layer that wraps the model and is responsible for calling tools and completing tasks.
An open protocol ecosystem that lets AI call external tools and data.
The ability for AI to operate web pages through the browser interface in place of a human.
The general ability for AI to directly control a graphical interface to complete tasks.
The information about you that AI can see, including history, preferences and the current task.
